gdp.title: Brejoin would bring back uncertainty, but less than the first time around
gdp.quote: The clearest damage from our departure is to goods trade. The value of UK goods exports fell by around £10 billion between 2019 and 2024, even as world goods exports grew by a quarter, and the UK had the largest fall in goods export volumes in the G7, as this first chart shows. Services have held up better – they made up 59 per cent of UK exports in 2024, up from 48 per cent in 2019 – but that’s from goods shrinking, rather than services growing. In fact, our services exports have only just kept pace with the rest of the G7. […] Add it all up and the hit to the economy may be bigger than expected before we breparted (sorry). The Office for Budget Responsibility assumes Brexit will eventually reduce productivity by around 4 per cent. We reckon GDP is already between 4 and 10 per cent lower.

gdp.title: Are We In The ‘Foothills’ Of AI-Driven Growth?
gdp.quote: It seems we finally have some good economic news to cheer about. GDP grew by 0.7 per cent in Q3, making the UK the second-fastest-growing economy in the G7, behind only the US. This was the fastest quarterly growth since the end of 2017 excluding the post-pandemic recovery (although growth at this rate was normal before the pandemic). So, in this post we dig into whether we are seeing the start of an AI-driven growth boom as some in government have claimed, drawing out the implications for the labour market and interest rates as well as the broader economy.

gdp.quote: The bigger story this week wasn’t the rate rise, it was the Bank’s new economic outlook. Inflation is now forecast to peak at 4.9 per cent next spring and not to get back to the 2 per cent target until the third quarter of 2028. gdp.title: Are We In The ‘Foothills’ Of AI-Driven Growth?
gdp.quote: The first place to look for the effect of AI is in the investment needed for its infrastructure. Spending on data centres, servers, semiconductors, connections to the power grid, and the software itself should show up as a boost to investment. In that context, it’s encouraging that investment has been strong in recent quarters – contributing around half of GDP growth in Q3. More compellingly, if we look at the assets that are being invested in – as shown in Figure 1 – it’s ICT equipment and buildings where investment is concentrated. So this picture is at least consistent with a growth bump from AI investment, albeit this is very much circumstantial evidence. It’s also important to stress that the contribution to UK GDP will depend on the extent to which this new infrastructure is imported, and how much is produced at home and in that context, it’s striking that net trade was a drag on GDP in the latest data. This is something that we should expect to continue.

unemp.title: Three figures we should all pay attention to in the Milburn Review
unemp.quote: The Milburn Review concludes that a combination of early intervention, improved health support, more education and training investment and active labour market policies would result in a ‘big bang’ when it comes to youth employment. By 2036-37, the Review estimates 440,000 more young people would be in employment as a result, and that this would save the state £2.4 billion in 2036-37 as higher taxes and lower benefits are paid. […] But achieving that outcome, too, may prove quite the task. Dividing the £5.8 billion of extra support by the 440,000 extra young people the report says will get into employment as a result suggests the average cost of getting each additional young person into work will be around £13,000. Sounds like a lot? It’s not. Past employment support schemes have spent around £30,000 per additional young person employed. Milburn’s £5.8 billion on employment, health and other support would have to be about three times as effective to get 440,000 additional young people into work.

unemp.title: Are We In The ‘Foothills’ Of AI-Driven Growth?
unemp.quote: The other potential dark cloud to the silver lining of AI-driven growth could come from the labour market. The context here is the warning issued this week from central banks that AI – among other factors – is leading to lower labour demand, putting downward pressure on hiring. Figure 5 provides some extra evidence here, showing that around one in ten businesses expect AI to reduce their headcount in the future, roughly double the 6 per cent already reporting AI-related reductions. By contrast, only 2 per cent anticipate a positive impact. In short, if we are in the foothills of AI-driven growth, then we are likely also at the very beginning of the labour market churn that comes with it.

unemp.title: It’s good to be flexible
unemp.quote: If the LPC had done something similar this year – continued closing the gap to the adult rate, with a target of 2029 – then the 18-20-year-old rate would have increased by roughly 10 per cent. But the Government has responded to flashing alarm bells in the youth labour market by relaxing (or clarifying) this part of the LPC’s remit too. The LPC was told explicitly it could choose the pace of the youth-adult convergence (i.e. ‘don’t fixate on 2029’) and that it should prioritise young people’s employment prospects. […] I thought this might lead to some convergence, albeit less than in recent years, resulting in a youth uprating just above the adult uprating. But the LPC paused convergence altogether. I think this was a good call. As I set out last week, we can’t say for sure that minimum wage increases are to blame for a deteriorating youth labour market, but we also can’t say that they are not, and it’s not worth taking the risk.

By contrast, the rate among 25-64-year-olds held up, reached a new high in 2023, and only then drifted down to 1 per cent below 2019 levels. So, the picture is pretty much the same as where we started. There has been a serious fall in youth employment since 2022, which isn’t accounted for by rising education participation, or by population or migration changes.

pop.title: Andy Burnham’s EU ‘reset’ deal highlights the problems of incrementalism
pop.quote: Opponents are arguing that these breach the UK’s red lines by effectively moving us inside the single market for agricultural goods, that the UK has become a rule taker by accepting the EU design of emissions trading, and that the YES is tantamount to freedom of movement through the backdoor. However, the UK parliament could still decide not to accept new EU rules (though at the price that access newly gained would be lost) and the YES is a souped up version of working holiday schemes that the UK already has with nations like Australia, Canada and South Korea. Indeed, the EU could say that 100,000 is proportionally very low compared to Australia’s 45,000 annual quota. The big concession will come when/if the UK discounts tuition fees for EU students at UK universities – something not conceded to any of these other countries. The language in the joint statement avoids pegging agreement to charging domestic fees and it remains to be seen whether the EU will settle for less.

earn.title: My final newsletter – fewer meetings, less management, slower pay growth?
earn.quote: It wouldn’t be a Mike TOTC without some mention of inequality, and yesterday’s ONS Annual Survey of Hours and Earnings data dump gave us the definitive take on earnings inequality, with data now up to 2026. The headline was that the share of workers in low pay failed to fall for the first time in 15 years, but Chart of the Week takes a closer look at overall pay inequality, measured by the 90:10 ratio (where higher numbers mean more unequal pay) for hourly pay and weekly earnings. Women’s weekly earnings have long been less equal than men’s – due to their higher share of part-time workers – but the genders have been slowly converging since this series began in 2002. More recently, overall earnings inequality has ticked up across the board, after a decade of decline. This is partly because the National Living Wage, which used to outpace median pay, is now only keeping pace with it, but is also because high earners are pulling away: weekly pay for the 90th percentile grew by 7.3 per cent in nominal terms this year (to reach £1,433 a week), against just 1.1 per cent at the 10th percentile. Among men, earnings inequality is now at its joint highest on record (alongside 2014), thanks to increasing numbers with a low weekly paycheck (the 10th percentile fell in cash terms from £309 in 2025 to £301 in 2026).

cpi.title: The Return of the Energy Shock
cpi.quote: We must state two things about this path clearly. The first is that the peak has moved up by almost a full percentage point since July, from 4.5 per cent to 5.4 per cent, while its timing has stayed put in the first quarter of 2027. That revision is almost entirely the energy channel doing what it is designed to do: the price of Brent crude oil is 50 per cent higher than when the July models were trained, UK wholesale gas prices have risen 78 per cent since the Bank’s July Report, and the Ofgem energy price cap has gone from £1,477 in Q2 to £1,663 in Q3 and £1,723 for October–December, with Cornwall Insight now forecasting £1,999, a 16 per cent rise, for January 2027. The second is that part of the January step is arithmetic rather than economics. The CPI fell by 0.5 per cent month-on-month in January 2026; so, roughly half a point of the first quarter peak is that base effect. It is real, in the sense that the headline rate will print it, but it does not imply a fresh burst of price pressure in that month.

gilt.title: How Is The UK’s Deficit Reduction Plan (Actually) Likely To Proceed?
gilt.quote: In this week’s blog, I set out what I think is a credible path for the UK’s public finances. I use the historical record of borrowing forecasts against outturns to discipline how the fiscal plans are likely to be revised in the years ahead. On this path, the primary balance improves but stays in deficit over the next five years. The current budget is in deficit by around £30 billion in 2029-30, so the fiscal rules are missed by a significant margin. The debt ratio rises throughout the forecast, reaching 101 per cent of GDP by 2031-32. My guess is that this is closer to the market’s expectation than the official forecast, and it may help resolve the puzzle of why the UK’s borrowing costs remain the highest in the G7 despite the IMF’s praise.

gilt.title: Breathing Space, Not a Strategy
gilt.quote: Today’s Budget has seen the Chancellor deliver some ‘breathing space’ to households struggling with cost-of-living pressures via a mild fiscal loosening, most obviously through changes to energy bills and council taxes. Against an already difficult domestic and international macroeconomic backdrop, which has created a strain on the public finances, the net effect of today’s measures has been a reduction in the Chancellor’s buffer against his fiscal rules from £23.6 billion in March to £14.5 billion now. Market reaction to the Budget was subsequently muted. Ten-year gilt yields fell by only a few basis points on Wednesday afternoon, while sterling hardly budged. gilt.title: The Minimal Credibility Test For The Autumn 2026 Budget
gilt.quote: Our assessment is that part of shock to global yields will dissipate if there is a resolution to the conflict in the middle east. The ten-year gilt yield has risen by around 110 basis points since the conflict began in February, to about 5.4 per cent, its highest since 2007, and the rise has been global. Roughly a third of the UK move reflects higher inflation compensation and the policy rates expected to deal with it. The rest is likely to prove persistent. The real rate the market prices for 2031 to 2036 has risen by 75 basis points in the UK and by almost 100 in the US. That is harder to square with a temporary energy shock story. It is easier to rationalise as a global shift in the real interest rate, driven by the AI investment boom and the scale of government borrowing everywhere, with a term premium on gilts that has been rising since July on top. Around two-thirds of the rise in borrowing costs, on this reckoning, is here to stay.

gas.title: Budget 2026 special
gas.quote: One of the Chancellor’s big choices was to use some of his insurance policy (letting the current budget that he has promised to balance fall from £24bn to £15bn). If things turn out better than expected this will prove a wise move. So far, however, it looks like the Chancellor’s chips are down. The OBR took economic data up to mid-August into account in its forecast. By Budget day, gas prices were far above the OBR’s central forecast and looked dangerously close to its “severe” shock scenario, while oil had climbed two-thirds of the way there. On energy prices, the OBR’s downside scenario is starting to look like the central case (though at our event this week Haskel explained that how long high prices are sustained for will be crucial). In that scenario, inflation tops 5 per cent next year. But the Government does get a sliver of good news. Although the severe scenario does show higher borrowing overall, that’s entirely down to a one percentage point rise in gilt yields that has not yet materialised. So while households are facing something like the severe scenario, the Treasury (for now at least) is not.

gas.title: The Return of the Energy Shock
gas.quote: We must state two things about this path clearly. The first is that the peak has moved up by almost a full percentage point since July, from 4.5 per cent to 5.4 per cent, while its timing has stayed put in the first quarter of 2027. That revision is almost entirely the energy channel doing what it is designed to do: the price of Brent crude oil is 50 per cent higher than when the July models were trained, UK wholesale gas prices have risen 78 per cent since the Bank’s July Report, and the Ofgem energy price cap has gone from £1,477 in Q2 to £1,663 in Q3 and £1,723 for October–December, with Cornwall Insight now forecasting £1,999, a 16 per cent rise, for January 2027. The second is that part of the January step is arithmetic rather than economics. The CPI fell by 0.5 per cent month-on-month in January 2026; so, roughly half a point of the first quarter peak is that base effect. It is real, in the sense that the headline rate will print it, but it does not imply a fresh burst of price pressure in that month.

ecb.title: Ahead of a presidential election, France first needs to help itself on debt
ecb.quote: Of all the sovereigns facing rising rates, France may face the biggest challenge. Today’s bond market is exposing a French economic problem that has been building for years. France has lost economic ground relative to Germany since about 2010, in a context of Germany’s own weak performance. More strikingly, France has lost ground relative to Italy since 2020 (Figure 1). France must grapple with structurally higher long-term interest rates in the context of a very weak fiscal starting point and a longstanding growth problem. Until now, French government bonds have enjoyed something close to a mini-exorbitant privilege, with yields just a little higher than Germany and in any case too big to fail. Public debt climbed from around the Maastricht-compatible 60 percent of GDP at the birth of the euro to 120 percent today, without governments being forced to confront the sustainability of public debt and the French social model.

ecb.quote: The French-German spread indicates how much of the bond repricing is specific to France relative to Germany, but the outright yield is the market variable that matters most for debt dynamics. It determines the marginal rate at which France refinances itself and, over time, the effective interest cost on the debt stock. The government now projects the debt-interest bill to rise from €79.2 billion in 2026 to €91.2 billion in 2027. With gross financing needs running into hundreds of billions of euros per year, a persistently higher clearing yield will gradually raise debt-service costs and make an already difficult fiscal adjustment harder.

This decline is driven by increased debt servicing costs, which are expected to strain disposable incomes. Economies with a high share of fixed-rate loans, such as France and Belgium, may experience some insulation from immediate impacts, while those with floating-rate loans, like Finland, could face greater challenges. The resilience of the labour market and household balance sheets will play crucial roles in mitigating potential downturns.

ecb.quote: The euro area is far better equipped for sovereign stress than it was in 2010-12, when concerns about government solvency spilled into banks and fragmented financing conditions across the currency union. Banks are now better capitalised, and the ECB has additional tools. But what the ECB can legitimately do in terms of bond purchases is narrow. Outright Monetary Transactions, under which the ECB could purchase short-term sovereign bonds, would require a European Stability Mechanism programme and associated conditionality for France. A French request for such a programme before the election is politically hard to imagine unless the crisis becomes extreme. […] That leaves the more-recent Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI) and other minor tweaks in current ECB policy and operations at the Governing Council’s disposal. The ECB could for instance decide to pause or slow the shrinking of its balance sheet in the face of rising yields across the euro area, similarly to the Bank of England for British government debt.

Unsurprisingly, the ICT sector leads the pack with 60 per cent of firms confirming their use of AI in the latest vintage, up from 30 per cent in the first. Professional services follow in second place, at two-fifths of firms. At the other end of the scale, fewer than 20 per cent of firms in the hospitality and construction sectors report AI usage. tfp.title: Are We In The ‘Foothills’ Of AI-Driven Growth?
tfp.quote: Seeing early signs of AI-related activity is particularly encouraging given that there are good reasons to think such gains should emerge slowly. Any company starting to use a new technology may initially see productivity fall given time taken to understand how to use the technology and, for example, make the complementary investments required to realise its potential. This includes significant complementary investments in intangible capital, including redesigning processes, training workers, restructuring the organisation and developing new products and approaches. This means AI may actively reduce measured output and productivity in the near term. But, as firms exploit the technology the gains should become apparent. Academic work for the US that digs into this AI J-curve finds that unmeasured intangible investment associated with computer hardware and software raises so-called total factor productivity. As Robert Solow put it during the ICT boom of the 1990s: “you can see the computer age everywhere but in the productivity statistics”

fiscal.quote: This week’s Budget, like its predecessors, assumes a sizeable fiscal squeeze in the years ahead. On the OBR’s numbers, the primary balance (tax receipts minus spending on everything except debt interest) is forecast to improve by 3 per cent of GDP over the next 5 years, from a deficit of 1.5 per cent in 2025-26 to a surplus of the same size by 2030-31. fiscal.title: How Is The UK’s Deficit Reduction Plan (Actually) Likely To Proceed?
fiscal.quote: In this week’s blog, I set out what I think is a credible path for the UK’s public finances. I use the historical record of borrowing forecasts against outturns to discipline how the fiscal plans are likely to be revised in the years ahead. On this path, the primary balance improves but stays in deficit over the next five years. The current budget is in deficit by around £30 billion in 2029-30, so the fiscal rules are missed by a significant margin. The debt ratio rises throughout the forecast, reaching 101 per cent of GDP by 2031-32. My guess is that this is closer to the market’s expectation than the official forecast, and it may help resolve the puzzle of why the UK’s borrowing costs remain the highest in the G7 despite the IMF’s praise.

If things turn out better than expected this will prove a wise move. So far, however, it looks like the Chancellor’s chips are down. The OBR took economic data up to mid-August into account in its forecast. By Budget day, gas prices were far above the OBR’s central forecast and looked dangerously close to its “severe” shock scenario, while oil had climbed two-thirds of the way there. On energy prices, the OBR’s downside scenario is starting to look like the central case (though at our event this week Haskel explained that how long high prices are sustained for will be crucial). In that scenario, inflation tops 5 per cent next year. But the Government does get a sliver of good news. Although the severe scenario does show higher borrowing overall, that’s entirely down to a one percentage point rise in gilt yields that has not yet materialised. So while households are facing something like the severe scenario, the Treasury (for now at least) is not.

fiscal.title: Breathing Space, Not a Strategy
fiscal.quote: Today’s Budget has seen the Chancellor deliver some ‘breathing space’ to households struggling with cost-of-living pressures via a mild fiscal loosening, most obviously through changes to energy bills and council taxes. Against an already difficult domestic and international macroeconomic backdrop, which has created a strain on the public finances, the net effect of today’s measures has been a reduction in the Chancellor’s buffer against his fiscal rules from £23.6 billion in March to £14.5 billion now. Market reaction to the Budget was subsequently muted. Ten-year gilt yields fell by only a few basis points on Wednesday afternoon, while sterling hardly budged. […] Therefore, while today’s Budget appears to have not resulted in a backlash from the markets, maintaining a backloaded path for tax rises and deferring major fiscal decisions on defence and other spending until the 2027 Spending Review to buy time is not a credible fiscal strategy.
